Mini-Lesson

Islam: Sources of Wisdom and Authority

4 missions. Guess, learn, then check. Your place is saved.

  1. Mission 1The Islamic calendar starts with a journey, not a birth. What made one escape so important?
  2. Mission 2Sunni and Shi'a Muslims both honour Ali. Why did one question in 632 divide them?
  3. Mission 3The Qur'an says "pray", but not exactly how. Where do Muslims learn the rest?
  4. Mission 4The Qur'an never mentions cocaine or cigarettes. How do Muslim scholars decide what Islam says?

Also part of this unit: 2 missions in Islam: Beliefs (part 1); 1 mission in Islam: Beliefs (part 2).

Mission 1

Mission 1: The Islamic calendar starts with a journey, not a birth. What made one escape so important?

Make a guess: The Islamic calendar starts with a journey, not a birth. What made one escape so important?

Mission 1

Makkah around 570 CE

  • Makkah: a trading town in a dry valley in western Arabia, ruled by the Quraysh tribe.
  • At its centre stood the Ka'bah. Muslims believe Ibrahim and Isma'il built it for the worship of the one God.
  • By the 6th century it was filled with idols of many tribal gods, and pilgrims to them brought trade.
  • Muslims call this time Jahiliyyah: the "age of ignorance".
  • Tribe and family decided who was protected; the poor, orphans and slaves had few rights.
Mission 1

An orphan called al-Amin

  • Muhammad was born in Makkah around 570 CE, into the Hashim clan of the Quraysh.
  • His father died before he was born; his mother died when he was about six.
  • He was raised by his grandfather, then by his uncle Abu Talib.
  • He worked as a shepherd, then as a trader on caravan journeys to Syria.
  • People called him al-Amin: "the trustworthy". Makkans left valuables with him for safe keeping.
  • He worked for Khadijah, a respected merchant; she proposed marriage, and they married when he was 25.
  • When the clans argued over who should replace the sacred Black Stone in the rebuilt Ka'bah, he set it on a cloak so every clan leader could lift it together.
Quick check
?Why did the people of Makkah call the young Muhammad al-Amin?
Mission 1Read the source

"Read!": the first revelation

  • Around 610 CE, aged 40, Muhammad often went to pray and reflect in the cave of Hira' on a mountain near Makkah.
  • One night in Ramadan, Muslims believe, the angel Jibril (Gabriel) came to him and commanded him to read or recite.

> "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth, Createth man from a clot. Read: And thy Lord is the Most Bounteous, Who teacheth by the pen, Teacheth man that which he knew not." (Surah 96:1–5, Pickthall)

Q1 Who does the passage say is the source of human knowledge?

Show answer

God, "thy Lord", who teaches by the pen.

Q2 Why might Muslims see "Read!" as a fitting first word of the Qur'an?

Show answer

The word Qur'an means "recitation"; the message is to be read and passed on.

Mission 1

After the cave: fear, comfort, a calling

  • Muhammad ran home shaking and asked to be wrapped up. Khadijah comforted him: God would not disgrace a man so kind and honest (paraphrase of a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari).
  • Her Christian cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal said the same angel who came to Moses had come to him.
  • After a pause, revelations continued for the rest of his life: about 23 years.
  • Significance: for Muslims, this is the start of Risalah in its final form: God speaks again to humanity, through a final messenger.
  • For Muslims, this shows the message came from God, not from Muhammad: he was afraid and did not seek it.
Mission 1

The first Muslims

  • For about three years Muhammad taught quietly, among family and friends.
  • Khadijah: the first person to accept Islam.
  • Ali ibn Abi Talib: his young cousin, raised in his house, about 10 years old.
  • Abu Bakr: a close friend and merchant; many Sunni sources call him the first adult free man to believe.
  • Zayd ibn Harithah: a freed slave whom Muhammad had adopted.
  • Traditions tell this differently: Sunni accounts stress Abu Bakr's early faith; Shi'a accounts stress that Ali was first among men, and that when the Prophet first called his clan to Islam, he named Ali his brother and successor.
Quick check
?Which statement about the first revelation in the cave of Hira' matches Muslim belief?
Mission 1

Why Makkah's leaders turned against him

  • From about 613 Muhammad preached in public. Most Quraysh leaders opposed him.
  • Religion: "God is one" attacked the idols, and the ways of their ancestors.
  • Money: pilgrims to the idols at the Ka'bah brought trade to Makkah.
  • Power: if all believers are equal before God, the tribe's leaders lose their status.
  • Justice: the message demanded care for the poor and orphans, and condemned cheating and greed.
  • Judgement: many mocked the idea that the dead would rise to be judged.
Mission 1

Ten hard years

  • Persecution: Bilal, an Abyssinian slave, was tortured with a rock on his chest; he kept repeating "One, One". Sumayyah was killed for her faith.
  • c. 615: some Muslims fled to Abyssinia (Ethiopia), where a Christian king protected them.
  • c. 616–619: a boycott of the Prophet's clan: no trade or marriage with them.
  • 619, the Year of Sorrow: Khadijah and Abu Talib both died. Without his uncle, the Prophet lost his clan's protection.
  • He sought support in Ta'if, and was driven out with stones.
  • c. 620: the Night Journey and Ascension (Isra' and Mi'raj): Muslims believe he was taken to Jerusalem and to heaven, and the five daily prayers were given.
Quick check
?Which reason best explains why Makkah's leaders saw the Prophet's message as a threat to their wealth?
Mission 1

The Hijrah, 622 CE

  • People from Yathrib, a town about 450 km north, accepted Islam and promised to protect the Prophet (the pledges of Aqabah).
  • Muslims moved there in small groups. The Quraysh plotted to kill him: "they plot, but Allah (also) plotteth" (Surah 8:30, Pickthall).
  • Ali slept in the Prophet's bed to fool the attackers. The Prophet and Abu Bakr hid in the cave of Thawr for three days: "when they two were in the cave… Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us." (Surah 9:40, Pickthall)
  • They reached Quba near Yathrib, where the first mosque was built, then entered the town.
  • Yathrib became Madinat al-Nabi, "the city of the Prophet": Madinah.
  • Hijrah means "migration". The migrants are the Muhajirun; the Madinans who welcomed them are the Ansar ("helpers").
Mission 1

Why the Hijrah still matters

  • Calendar: the Islamic calendar counts from 622: year 1 AH (anno Hegirae, "in the year of the Hijrah"). The caliph Umar chose it.
  • Why not his birth or the first revelation? The Hijrah began the first Muslim community (ummah) living by God's guidance.
  • Turning point: from a persecuted minority to a community with its own mosque, leaders and laws.
  • Example: Muslims see it as a model of sacrifice: leaving home, wealth and family for God.
  • Brotherhood: the Ansar shared homes and wealth with the Muhajirun; many Muslims point to this when they welcome refugees today.
Mission 1Evaluate

"The Hijrah was more important than the first revelation."

  • For: the Hijrah turned believers into a community (ummah) with a mosque, leaders and laws. Islam survived and spread from Madinah. The calendar starts there.
  • Against: without the revelation there would be no Islam to migrate for. Hira' is the start of the Qur'an, the source of all later guidance. Many Muslims mark Laylat al-Qadr as "better than a thousand months" (Surah 97:3).
  • Another view: the events cannot be ranked: the Prophet's life is one whole, and Muslims follow his whole example (Sunnah).
  • Judge it by: Important for what: belief, community or history? What do Muslims remember and celebrate today? Could either have happened without the other?
Mission check

?A Muslim charity in Britain names its project for welcoming refugees "Ansar". What does this name show about how Muslims understand the Hijrah?

The Hijrah turned a persecuted group into a community. That is why the Islamic calendar begins there. A later mission: Madinah, and the Seal of the Prophets.

Mission 2

Mission 2: Sunni and Shi'a Muslims both honour Ali. Why did one question in 632 divide them?

Make a guess: Sunni and Shi'a Muslims both honour Ali. Why did one question in 632 divide them?

Mission 2

632: who leads now?

  • The Prophet died in June 632. He had been prophet, judge and leader of the Muslim community (ummah).
  • No new prophet would come. But who would lead?
  • One answer: the community chooses the best-qualified Muslim. Those who followed this became the Sunni Muslims: "people of the Sunnah and the community".
  • Another answer: God had already chosen a leader from the Prophet's family, through the Prophet: his cousin and son-in-law Ali. His supporters were the Shi'at Ali, "the party of Ali": Shi'a Muslims.
  • At first the question was about leadership. Over time it shaped belief, law and worship.
Mission 2

Abu Bakr chosen

  • While Ali and the Prophet's family prepared his burial, leaders of Madinah met at the Saqifah (a meeting hall).
  • Umar pledged loyalty (bay'ah) to Abu Bakr; most of those present followed. Abu Bakr became the first caliph (khalifah: successor).
  • Sunni view: a right choice by consultation (shura): Abu Bakr was the Prophet's closest friend, his companion in the cave, and led the prayers in the Prophet's last illness.
  • Shi'a view: the meeting ignored the Prophet's choice. Ali and the family were absent.
  • Ali later gave his pledge to Abu Bakr: Sunni sources present this as agreement; Shi'a sources, as accepting what he could not change, for the sake of unity.
Mission 2

Ghadir Khumm: two readings

  • March 632: returning from the Farewell Pilgrimage, the Prophet stopped at the pool (ghadir) of Khumm, took Ali's hand and said: for whoever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla (paraphrase of a hadith in Sunni and Shi'a collections).
  • Mawla can mean "master, leader" or "friend, ally".
  • Shi'a reading: "master": a public appointment of Ali as leader after him. This is nass: explicit designation of the next Imam, by God's command through the Prophet.
  • Shi'a Muslims link it to Surah 5:67, "O Messenger! Make known that which hath been revealed unto thee from thy Lord" (Pickthall), and to 5:3, "This day have I perfected your religion for you" (Pickthall).
  • Sunni reading: "friend": the Prophet answered complaints about Ali and told Muslims to love and support him; it was not about the caliphate.
  • Shi'a Muslims celebrate the day as Eid al-Ghadir.
Quick check
?Which statement correctly describes the Shi'a view of what happened at Ghadir Khumm?
Mission 2Read the source

The Household: Surah 33:33

  • Surah 33:32 begins "O ye wives of the Prophet!" (Pickthall) and gives them guidance.

> "Allah's wish is but to remove uncleanness far from you, O Folk of the Household, and cleanse you with a thorough cleansing." (Surah 33:33, Pickthall)

  • Ahl al-Bayt: "people of the House": the Prophet's family.
  • Your course spells it Ahl-ul-Bayt.
  • Shi'a reading: this sentence is about the five "people of the cloak": Muhammad, Ali, Fatimah, Hasan and Husayn. A hadith tells of the Prophet covering them with his cloak and reciting it. God has purified them: a basis for belief that the Imams are protected from sin (inerrant;).
  • Sunni reading: in its setting it includes the Prophet's wives, and also Ali, Fatimah and their sons (many Sunni scholars accept the hadith of the cloak, which is in Sahih Muslim). It honours the family; it does not make them leaders or sinless.

Q1 Whom does 33:32 address?

Show answer

The Prophet's wives.

Q2 Why does the meaning of "Household" matter for authority?

Show answer

If it means the five, purified by God, Shi'a Muslims see the Imams' authority rooted in the Qur'an.

Mission 2

The caliphs: Abu Bakr and Umar

  • Abu Bakr (632–634):
    • Defeated tribes that broke away or refused zakah (the Ridda wars), keeping Arabia united.
    • Ordered the first written collection of the Qur'an.
    • Named Umar to follow him.
  • Umar (634–644):
    • Islam spread to Syria, Jerusalem (637), Iraq, Persia and Egypt.
    • Began the Hijri calendar; set up a register (diwan) to pay soldiers and support the poor; took the title "Commander of the Faithful".
    • Known for strict justice and a simple life. Killed in 644; he left a council (shura) of six to choose the next caliph.
Mission 2

The caliphs: Uthman and Ali

  • Uthman (644–656):
    • Made the standard written copy of the Qur'an and sent it to the main cities.
    • Further expansion; the first Muslim navy.
    • Criticised for appointing relatives (the Umayyad clan) as governors; killed by rebels in Madinah in 656.
  • Ali (656–661):
    • Ruled from Kufa (Iraq) amid the first civil war (fitna): the Battle of the Camel (656); Siffin (657) against Mu'awiya, governor of Syria.
    • Remembered for justice, learning and eloquence; his sermons and letters are gathered in Nahj al-Balaghah.
    • Killed in 661 by an extremist (a Kharijite) in the mosque at Kufa.
  • After Ali, Mu'awiya founded the Umayyad dynasty. In 680 Ali's son Husayn was killed at Karbala.
  • Sunni: the four are the Rightly-Guided Caliphs (al-Khulafa' al-Rashidun). Shi'a: Ali is the first rightful Imam; he advised the first three, but they were not the Prophet's appointed successors.
Quick check
?Which caliph is matched with one of his achievements?
Mission 2

Two traditions today

  • Sunni Muslims (about 87–90% of Muslims): leadership by the best-qualified, chosen by the community; authority in the Qur'an, the Sunnah and the scholars.
  • Shi'a Muslims (about 10–13%): the imamate (Imamah): leadership belongs to Imams from the Prophet's family, appointed by God through nass, beginning with Ali.
  • Role of the Imam (Shi'a): to guide the community without error, to interpret the Qur'an, to keep the Prophet's teaching pure.
  • Significance: for Shi'a Muslims, Imamah is a root of faith (Usul ad-Din); Shi'a groups include Twelvers (the largest), Isma'ilis and Zaydis (whose view of the imamate is less strict).
  • Shared: one God, the Qur'an, the Prophet; prayer, fasting, zakah and Hajj (Sunni Muslims call these acts, with the Shahadah, the Five Pillars). Sunni Muslims also love the Prophet's family: every salah sends blessings on "Muhammad and the family of Muhammad".
Mission 2

The Prophet's family in Ismaili Islam

  • Isma'ilis follow the line of Imams through Isma'il, son of the sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sadiq.
  • Nizari Isma'ilis believe there is always a living, present Imam, a direct descendant of the Prophet through Ali and Fatimah.
  • The present Imam, Aga Khan V, became the 50th Imam in 2025.
  • The Imam of the time interprets the faith for each age: so for Isma'ilis the Ahl al-Bayt is a present source of guidance, not only a past one.
  • Musta'li Isma'ilis (e.g. the Dawoodi Bohras) believe their Imam is in hiding; they are led by a representative, the Da'i al-Mutlaq.
Quick check
?Which belief is held by Shi'a Muslims but not by Sunni Muslims?
Mission 2Evaluate

"The split between Sunni and Shi'a Muslims was only about politics."

  • For: it began with a practical question: who leads the community? Both share the Qur'an, the Prophet, prayer, fasting, zakah and Hajj. Ali himself worked with the first three caliphs.
  • Against: for Shi'a Muslims the leader is chosen by God, and Imamah is a root of faith. The two traditions developed different hadith collections, schools of law and practices (e.g. Ashura). Readings of the Qur'an (33:33) and Hadith (Ghadir Khumm) differ.
  • Another view: it began as a question of authority, which in Islam is both religious and political, so the two cannot be separated.
  • Judge it by: Is choosing a leader a religious question in Islam? How much do the differences affect worship and belief today? How do Sunni and Shi'a Muslims describe the split themselves?
Mission check

?Sunni and Shi'a students plan a joint assembly about Ali ibn Abi Talib. Which statement could both groups share without disagreement?

Both traditions honour Ali. They divided over whether the Prophet's successor was chosen by the community or appointed by God.

Mission 3

Mission 3: The Qur'an says "pray", but not exactly how. Where do Muslims learn the rest?

Make a guess: The Qur'an says "pray", but not exactly how. Where do Muslims learn the rest?

Mission 3

Sunnah and Hadith

  • Sunnah ("path" or "custom"): the Prophet Muhammad's way of life: what he said, what he did, and what he approved by staying silent.
  • Hadith ("report", "news"; plural ahadith): a report, passed on orally and later in writing, of something in the Sunnah.
  • So the Sunnah is the example; the Hadith are how Muslims know it.
  • The Qur'an is God's word; a hadith records the Prophet's words and actions. Muslims keep them clearly apart.
Mission 3Read the source

Why follow the Prophet's example?

> "Verily in the messenger of Allah ye have a good example for him who looketh unto Allah and the Last Day" (Surah 33:21, Pickthall)

> "And whatsoever the messenger giveth you, take it. And whatsoever he forbiddeth, abstain (from it)." (Surah 59:7, Pickthall)

  • God sent the Qur'an to the Prophet "that thou mayst explain to mankind that which hath been revealed for them" (Surah 16:44, Pickthall).
  • "Obey Allah, and obey the messenger" (Surah 4:59, Pickthall).

Q1 According to 16:44, what was one task of the Prophet?

Show answer

To explain the revelation to people.

Q2 Why do these verses give the Sunnah authority?

Show answer

The Qur'an itself tells Muslims to obey and copy the Prophet.

Mission 3

Inside a hadith: isnad and matn

  • Every hadith has two parts:
  • Isnad ("support"): the chain of narrators, from the collector back to the Prophet.
  • Matn ("text"): the content: what the Prophet said or did.
  • Example (the first hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari):
  • Isnad: al-Bukhari ← al-Humaydi ← Sufyan ← Yahya ibn Sa'id ← Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ← Alqamah ← the caliph Umar ← the Prophet.
  • Matn: deeds are judged by their intentions, and each person will have what they intended (paraphrase).
  • A sound chain is unbroken, and every narrator in it is honest and has a good memory.
Quick check
?In a hadith, what is the isnad?
Mission 3

Testing and collecting

  • In the Prophet's lifetime, companions memorised his words; some wrote them down.
  • Later, false reports spread, so scholars of hadith (muhaddithun) travelled widely to collect and test them.
  • Testing the isnad: Did each narrator meet the next? Were they honest, careful, of good memory?
  • Testing the matn: Does it contradict the Qur'an, or better-known hadith?
  • Grades (Sunni scholars): sahih (sound) · hasan (good) · da'if (weak) · mawdu' (fabricated).
  • The great collections were made mainly in the 9th and 10th centuries CE.
Mission 3

Sunni collections

  • Sahih al-Bukhari: compiled by Muhammad al-Bukhari (810–870). He is said to have examined hundreds of thousands of reports and kept only those meeting his strictest tests.
  • Sahih Muslim: compiled by Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (d. 875).
  • Together, "the two Sahihs": for Sunni Muslims, the most trusted books after the Qur'an.
  • With four more (Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah) they form the Six Books.
  • Most Sunni hadith come through the companions (sahabah), such as Abu Hurayrah, Aisha and Umar.
Mission 3

Shi'a hadith: the Four Books

  • Shi'a Muslims follow the Prophet's Sunnah too, but trust it most when it comes through his family, the Ahl al-Bayt.
  • The sayings of the twelve Imams also carry authority: Shi'a Muslims believe the Imams were protected from error and handed down the Prophet's knowledge.
  • The Four Books:
  • al-Kafi, by al-Kulayni (d. 941)
  • Man la yahduruhu al-faqih, by al-Shaykh al-Saduq (d. 991)
  • Tahdhib al-ahkam and al-Istibsar, both by al-Shaykh al-Tusi (d. 1067)
  • Most Shi'a scholars hold that no collection is entirely sound: each report is still judged one by one.
Quick check
?Which statement about hadith collections in Sunni and Shi'a Islam is accurate?
Mission 3

The traditions of the companions

  • Companions (sahabah): Muslims who knew the Prophet and died as Muslims.
  • Sunni view: the companions as a whole are trustworthy narrators. The practice of the first four caliphs also guides Muslims: e.g. Umar gathered Muslims to pray tarawih together in Ramadan.
  • Shi'a view: companions are judged one by one. Many were faithful; some opposed Ali and the Prophet's family, so their reports are treated with caution.
  • Both honour companions such as Salman al-Farsi and Bilal.
  • Purpose: the companions show how the first Muslims lived the Prophet's example.
Mission 3

The Sunnah in daily life

  • Worship: the Qur'an says "establish worship"; the Sunnah shows how: wudu, the times, the number of rak'ahs, the words. The Prophet told Muslims to pray as they had seen him pray (hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, paraphrase).
  • Pillars: the 2.5% rate of zakah and the steps of Hajj come from the Sunnah.
  • Manners: saying "Bismillah" before eating, eating with the right hand, greeting with "As-salamu alaykum".
  • Character: none of you truly believes until he wants for his brother what he wants for himself (paraphrase of a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim).
  • Extra acts: voluntary prayers and fasts that the Prophet kept.
  • Law: the Sunnah, after the Qur'an, is a main source of Shari'ah (see Mission 4).
Mission 3Diversity

How much authority do the Hadith have?

  • Most Sunni and Shi'a Muslims: the Sunnah is the second source after the Qur'an and is needed to understand it.
  • Sunni: the two Sahihs are highly trusted; scholars still discuss individual reports in other books.
  • Shi'a: the Imams' teaching is part of the Sunnah; even the Four Books are checked report by report.
  • Qur'anists (a small minority): follow the Qur'an alone, doubting the Hadith's reliability. Most Muslims reject this: without the Sunnah, they say, salah could not be performed.
  • Some modern scholars: re-examine weaker hadith, e.g. on women's roles, while keeping the Sunnah's authority.
Quick check
?Why do most Muslims say the Qur'an cannot be fully practised without the Sunnah?
Mission 3Evaluate

"Muslims could not practise Islam without the Hadith."

  • For: the Qur'an tells Muslims to obey and follow the Prophet (4:59, 59:7, 33:21). Salah, zakah and Hajj depend on details found only in the Sunnah. The Prophet's role was to explain the Qur'an (16:44).
  • Against: the Qur'an is God's complete word; it calls itself clear guidance. Hadith were collected about two centuries later, and some reports are weak or fabricated. Qur'anists practise using the Qur'an alone.
  • Another view: the Sunnah is essential, but it was also passed on by practice, generation to generation, not only by written Hadith.
  • Judge it by: What does the Qur'an itself say about the Prophet's authority? How reliable is the testing of hadith? Is "practising Islam" the same as following every detail?
Mission check

?A social-media post shares a "hadith" saying that eating dates on Tuesdays brings wealth. It gives no chain of narrators and is in no known collection. How would most Muslim scholars treat it?

The Sunnah shows how to live the Qur'an. The isnad is how Muslims test whether a report really goes back to the Prophet.

Mission 4

Mission 4: The Qur'an never mentions cocaine or cigarettes. How do Muslim scholars decide what Islam says?

Make a guess: The Qur'an never mentions cocaine or cigarettes. How do Muslim scholars decide what Islam says?

Mission 4

Shari'ah: the straight path

  • Shari'ah means a "path", originally the path to water: the straight path God sets for life.
  • "And now have We set thee (O Muhammad) on a clear road of (Our) commandment; so follow it" (Surah 45:18, Pickthall).
  • It covers everything: worship, food, family, business, crime and manners.
  • It is both a code of behaviour and ethics and, where applied, a legal system.
  • Muslims believe Shari'ah is God's law; fiqh ("understanding") is the scholars' work of working out what it requires. Fiqh is human, so scholars can differ.
  • Purpose: to please God and to protect what matters: religion, life, mind, family and property.
Mission 4

Where the law comes from

  • 1. Qur'an: for Muslims, God's word, the first and highest source.
  • 2. Sunnah: the Prophet's example, recorded in the Hadith (see Mission 3).
  • 3. Ijma: consensus: the agreement of qualified scholars.
  • 4. Qiyas: analogy: applying a known ruling to a new case with the same cause.
  • Ijtihad: the scholar's careful effort of reasoning that uses these sources.
  • Shi'a (Ja'fari) law: Qur'an; Sunnah of the Prophet and the Imams; ijma, valued when it includes the Imam's view; and 'aql (reason) in place of qiyas.
Quick check
?Which statement correctly describes the sources of Shari'ah for most Sunni Muslims?
Mission 4Read the source

Consensus: Surah 4:115

> "And whoso opposeth the messenger after the guidance (of Allah) hath been manifested unto him, and followeth other than the believer's way, We appoint for him that unto which he himself hath turned" (Surah 4:115, Pickthall)

  • Sunni reading: the scholar al-Shafi'i (767–820) argued that "the believers' way" means the agreed way of the community: so ijma binds Muslims. A hadith adds that the community will not agree on an error (paraphrase).
  • Shi'a reading: consensus counts because, and when, it includes the view of the infallible Imam; agreement alone is not enough.
  • Example of ijma: the companions agreed to gather the Qur'an into one book.

Q1 What two things does the verse warn against?

Show answer

Opposing the messenger; following a way other than the believers'.

Q2 Why might Shi'a Muslims hesitate to make "the believers' way" mean any majority view?

Show answer

They hold that the majority went wrong over the succession after the Prophet.

Mission 4

Analogy (qiyas): a worked example

  • Qiyas applies an existing ruling to a new case that shares the same cause.
  • Original case: wine (khamr) is forbidden: "Strong drink and games of chance… are only an infamy of Satan's handiwork. Leave it aside" (Surah 5:90, Pickthall).
  • Cause: it intoxicates, clouding the mind. The Prophet said every intoxicant counts as khamr (paraphrase of a hadith in Sahih Muslim).
  • New case: cocaine, cannabis, whisky: none named in the Qur'an, but each intoxicates.
  • Ruling: haram (forbidden), by analogy.
  • This shows the chain: Qur'an → Hadith → Shari'ah ruling.
  • Shi'a jurists reject free analogy, but reach the same ruling here, because the hadith states the cause.
Mission 4

Ijtihad: reasoning out new answers

  • Ijtihad ("effort", "intellectual struggle"): a qualified scholar (mujtahid) reasons from the sources to a ruling.
  • When the Prophet sent Mu'adh ibn Jabal to Yemen as a judge, Mu'adh said he would judge by the Qur'an, then the Sunnah, then his own reasoning; the Prophet approved (paraphrase of a hadith in Abu Dawud).
  • Sunni: from about the 10th century many said the "gate of ijtihad" was closed and followed their school (taqlid: following). Many modern scholars use ijtihad again for new questions.
  • Shi'a: ijtihad never closed. Each Twelver Shi'a follows a living senior scholar, a marja' al-taqlid ("source to follow").
Quick check
?Many modern scholars rule that smoking is haram because it seriously harms health, and the Qur'an forbids self-destruction. Which method is this?
Mission 4

The schools of law

  • A madhhab is a school of fiqh, named after its founder. The four Sunni schools accept one another as valid.
  • Hanafi (Abu Hanifa, d. 767): the largest; Turkey, South and Central Asia, many British Muslims.
  • Maliki (Malik ibn Anas, d. 795): North and West Africa.
  • Shafi'i (al-Shafi'i, d. 820): Egypt, East Africa, South-East Asia.
  • Hanbali (Ahmad ibn Hanbal, d. 855): Saudi Arabia, Qatar; known for keeping closely to the texts of the Qur'an and Hadith.
  • Ja'fari (Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, d. 765): Twelver Shi'a; Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Bahrain.
  • Differences are mostly in detail: e.g. where the hands rest in salah; Shi'a Muslims often combine the five prayers into three times of day.
Mission 4

Ulema and qadis

  • Ulema (also spelt 'ulama'; singular 'alim, "one who knows"): scholars trained in Arabic, Qur'an, Hadith and fiqh. They teach, and a mufti among them gives a fatwa (a reasoned ruling).
  • Qadi: a judge who applies Shari'ah in a court. The Prophet and the early caliphs appointed judges (e.g. Mu'adh in Yemen).
  • Sunni: there are no priests; authority comes from learning. Muslims may ask different scholars.
  • Shi'a: the marja' has wide authority. In Iran, a senior jurist leads the state (wilayat al-faqih); many Shi'a scholars reject this political role.
  • Examples of rulings: many scholars, including a UK Muslim law council (1995), have ruled that organ donation is permitted to save life; others forbid it. Many recent fatwas declare smoking haram.
Mission 4

Halal and haram: a scale

  • Halal: permitted. Haram: forbidden.
  • Scholars place actions on a five-point scale:
  • Fard / wajib (obligatory): e.g. salah, fasting in Ramadan.
  • Mustahabb (recommended): e.g. extra prayers, smiling at others.
  • Mubah (neutral, simply allowed): e.g. what colour to wear.
  • Makruh (disliked): e.g. wasting water, even during wudu.
  • Haram (forbidden): e.g. pork, alcohol, theft, lying.
  • Principles: in daily matters, everything is halal unless forbidden. In real necessity the forbidden may be allowed: "he who is driven by necessity… it is no sin for him" (Surah 2:173, Pickthall).
Quick check
?A Muslim scholar describes eating with the left hand as makruh. What does this mean?
Mission 4Diversity

Shari'ah in different communities

  • For most Muslims, mainly personal: prayer, fasting, food, modesty, honest business, family life.
  • Muslim-majority countries differ: many base family law (marriage, divorce, inheritance) on Shari'ah; a few, such as Saudi Arabia and Iran, also apply Shari'ah in criminal law; some, such as Turkey, have secular law.
  • In the UK: Muslims keep UK law; many scholars teach that Muslims should keep their agreements with the country they live in. Islamic finance avoids interest; Shari'ah councils give religious rulings, mostly on Islamic divorce, which are not binding in UK law.
  • Debates among Muslims: how far ijtihad should go; whether old rulings fit modern society; the role of Shari'ah councils.
Mission 4Evaluate

"Shari'ah can guide Muslims today as well as it did in the Prophet's time."

  • For: its sources are God's word and the Prophet's example, believed to be for all times. Qiyas and ijtihad answer new questions (drugs, smoking, organ donation). Millions find it guides daily life.
  • Against: much fiqh was worked out in medieval societies. Scholars and schools disagree, so there is often no single answer. Muslims in non-Muslim countries live mainly under secular law.
  • Another view: the purposes of Shari'ah (protecting religion, life, mind, family and property) are timeless; some detailed rulings may need fresh ijtihad.
  • Judge it by: Is Shari'ah mainly personal ethics or state law? Does disagreement weaken it or show it is flexible? Who has authority to decide: ulema, marja' or individual conscience?
Mission check

?A new synthetic drug, unknown until last year, makes users intoxicated. Neither the Qur'an nor the Hadith names it. How would most Muslim scholars reach a ruling on it?

Shari'ah reaches new questions by reasoning from the Qur'an and Sunnah: that is how a modern drug can be haram without being named.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Muhammad (born c. 570 in Makkah) was an orphan, a trader and known as al-Amin, "the trustworthy".
  • In 610, in the cave of Hira', Muslims believe Jibril brought the first revelation: "Read!" (Surah 96:1–5).
  • The Quraysh persecuted the Muslims for religious, economic and political reasons; in 622 the Prophet made the Hijrah to Madinah, year 1 of the Islamic calendar.

Mission 2

  • In 632 the question "who leads?" had two answers: chosen by the community (Sunni: Abu Bakr, then Umar, Uthman, Ali) or appointed by God from the Prophet's family (Shi'a: Ali, by nass at Ghadir Khumm).
  • The four Rightly-Guided Caliphs united Arabia, spread Islam, standardised the Qur'an and faced the first civil war.
  • Surah 33:33 and the Ahl al-Bayt are read differently; Isma'ilis follow a living Imam of the Prophet's family.

Mission 3

  • The Sunnah is the Prophet's example (words, actions, approvals); a hadith is a report of it, made of an isnad (chain) and a matn (content).
  • Sunni Muslims trust the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari, Muslim) most; Shi'a Muslims use the Four Books, with the Imams' teaching passed through the Ahl al-Bayt.
  • For Muslims, the Sunnah is the second source of guidance and law: it shows how to pray, give and live.

Mission 4

  • For Muslims, Shari'ah ("straight path") is God's law for all of life; fiqh is the scholars' understanding of it.
  • Sunni sources: Qur'an, Sunnah, ijma (consensus), qiyas (analogy); Shi'a: Qur'an, Sunnah of the Prophet and Imams, ijma with the Imam, 'aql. Actions run from fard to haram.
  • Ulema and qadis interpret and apply it; schools and communities differ in detail and in how far it is state law.
